Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood CSM), Sam Chen (LumiHealth CTO), Maya Lopez (Infra), Dr. Robert King (Security), Evan Park (ML Eng)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on benchmark results vs the baseline provider. Redwood presented latency and throughput numbers for hosted and dedicated setups; notable improvements at p50/p95 and throughput with quantization + KV cache. Customer raised concerns about cold-starts, tail latencies, and SOC2/KMS integration for pilot. Agreed next steps: share raw logs/spreadsheet, run 24h sustained dedicated benchmark, customer to share traffic profile, schedule security deep-dive.
topics: KV cache / warm vs cold behavior
Next steps and pilot commercial terms
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're on for 55 minutes today, quick agenda — run through the benchmark results vs the baseline provider, discuss tuning (quantization, batching, cache), and agree next steps.
[00:18] Sam Chen: yep thanks Alex, we looked at the summary you sent, curious to understand the p99 numbers, we care a lot about tail latencies for user-facing chat.
[00:30] Priya Patel: sure, quick context — we ran the same prompt corpus you provided across both Redwood hosted and BaselineCloud with identical model checkpoint (unified-7b-fp16), measurements taken over 2 hours steady-state plus cold-start samples. baseline had more variability.
[00:48] Evan Park: quick Q — were you using q4 or fp16 for the quant runs?
[00:55] Priya Patel: for the quantized runs we used q4_0 for a latency-focused profile and q3 for the cost run; we kept fp16 for quality baseline.
[01:05] Maya Lopez: can you give the headline numbers?
[01:12] Priya Patel: yeah — so hosted Redwood p50 ~ 42ms, p95 ~ 98ms, p99 ~ 180-200ms depending on sequence length. BaselineCloud p50 ~ 70ms, p95 ~ 180ms, p99 ~ 360ms. Throughput wise, tokens/sec at peak for Redwood hosted was about 6k tokens/sec (with batching tuned), BaselineCloud averaged ~3.2k tokens/sec under the same request mix.
[01:45] Sam Chen: ok that's a decent delta, but the p99 numbers still feel high at 200ms — our SLA target is p99 < 150ms for 4k concurrent users, is that realistic?
[02:00] Priya Patel: depends on deployment — for that SLA we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity, and using KV prefix caching for repeated prompts. On Dedicated with q4 and aggressive batching we measured p99 ~120-140ms under load similar to your profile (we ran a 1 hour stress test).
[02:18] Dr. Robert King: what about cold-starts and the tail — if a node scales up from zero, we're worried about 2-4s spikes seen in other providers.
[02:30] Priya Patel: good point — Redwood autoscaler keeps a warm pool by default for dedicated pools; cold-starts on hosted can hit multi-second for large weights, but for your pilot we can configure always-on nodes and a warm cache which reduced cold spike to ~200-300ms in our tests. The baseline provider still had >1.2s cold spikes in our runs.
[02:55] Alex Rivera: also worth calling out kernel selection — our runtime chooses kernels based on seq len and hardware, that helps keep the long-tail lower than the naive provider.
[03:08] Evan Park: did you account for KV cache hits in the throughput numbers?
[03:12] Priya Patel: yes — the 6k tokens/sec was with prefix KV cache enabled (about 35% cache hit rate on that test corpus). Without cache it drops to ~4k. Baseline provider didn't have the same prefix caching enabled in their default config, so their numbers there were worse.
[03:34] Maya Lopez: curious on variance across instance types — are these measurements on A100s?
[03:40] Priya Patel: tests were on V100-equivalent for BaselineCloud and A10/A40 equivalent for Redwood hosted; Dedicated numbers we showed were on 2x H100s in our lab. We can provide the full GPU counters in the spreadsheet.
[03:58] Sam Chen: so bottom line — Redwood shows ~2x throughput and ~2x better p99 vs Baseline in your runs, but we need sustained runs and production-like traffic to validate.
[04:12] Priya Patel: agreed. One caveat — quantization can change generation quality slightly; we ran an eval sweep on your eval set and q4 preserved quality within 0.8% ROUGE/LL diff vs fp16 for the tasks you care about.
[04:31] Evan Park: good to know. On the security side, we need KMS/HSM integration and RBAC audit logs for pilot. Dr. King — any additions?
[04:40] Dr. Robert King: yes, SOC2 report and KMS key control are musts; we also need encryption-in-transit certs and retention policy. Also, do you capture prompt-level audit logs?
[04:52] Jordan Kim: we do — Redwood Console can export per-request metadata and token-level cost/latency. We can enable log shipping to your SIEM; will send the SOC2 and a short doc on KMS options.
[05:05] Dr. Robert King: great, we'll review.
[05:08] Maya Lopez: another practical item — network egress; BaselineCloud included egress fees baked into their quote, are there differences with Redwood Dedicated?
[05:18] Alex Rivera: for Dedicated we typically bill compute separately and can include an egress cap in the pilot contract; we'll have Jordan include options in the commercial terms.
[05:26] Priya Patel: back to benchmarks — we also measured latency distribution by sequence length, shorter inputs (<=128 tokens) had p99 ~110-130ms on Dedicated q4, longer sequences (512) pushed p99 toward 220-260ms. Baseline was consistently higher across lengths.
[05:47] Sam Chen: timeline thoughts — after you share the raw logs, we should run the 24h sustained test on Prod-like traffic, and then a joint readout. We want to finalize pilot commercial terms by mid-November.
[06:01] Alex Rivera: sounds good — action items summarized at end. Anything else on tuning?
[06:06] Evan Park: one more — how deterministic are the performance gains with mixed batching? Our traffic is bursty and often has pinned low-latency requests mixed with high-throughput background tasks.
[06:16] Priya Patel: Redwood supports route and policy-based routing — you can split critical low-latency requests to a latency-optimized pool (smaller batch sizes, dedicated nodes) and background higher-throughput requests to a cost-optimized pool (larger batching, quant). We can demo that routing in the next call.
[06:33] Maya Lopez: that would be helpful.
[06:36] Alex Rivera: ok we'll follow up. Recap and next steps: Alex shares spreadsheet + logs; Priya runs 24h dedicated benchmark and attaches GPU counters; Maya sends production traffic histogram; Jordan drafts pilot terms and includes dedicated burst option; security deep-dive scheduled.
[06:55] Alex Rivera: cool, thanks everyone — we'll get those over this week, talk soon.
[07:00] (meeting ends)
